topic_description: intersectional fairness evaluation in LLM-based recommender systems using CFaiRLLM with preference alignment and diverse user profile sampling strategies

Intersectional Fairness Preference Align.Problem: LLM-based recommender systems often perpetuate or amplify biases across multiple intersecting demographic attributes, leading to unfair recommendations for marginalized groups.
Intersectional Fairness Preference Align.Existing Methods: Current approaches focus on single-attribute fairness or use simple demographic parity metrics. The CFaiRLLM benchmark evaluates fairness on individual attributes but lacks intersectional analysis.
Intersectional Fairness Preference Align.Motivation: Intersectional fairness is crucial for capturing the compounded effects of multiple overlapping identities. By aligning LLM preferences with intersectional fairness criteria, we can create more equitable recommendation systems.
Intersectional Fairness Preference Align.Proposed Method: We introduce Intersectional Fairness Preference Alignment (IFPA), a novel approach combining preference learning and intersectional fairness optimization. First, we generate a diverse set of synthetic user profiles with intersecting attributes (e.g., age, gender, race, socioeconomic status). We then use these profiles to create pairwise preference data, where the preferred option is the one that maximizes an intersectional fairness metric (e.g., minimal group disparity across all intersecting groups). This preference data is used to fine-tune the LLM using techniques like Direct Preference Optimization. Additionally, we propose an intersectional fairness loss that encourages equal treatment across all combinations of protected attributes during training. At inference time, we employ a fairness-aware decoding strategy that adjusts output probabilities based on the intersectional fairness of candidate recommendations.
Intersectional Fairness Preference Align.Experiment Plan: We will evaluate IFPA on multiple recommendation domains (e.g., movies, books, job postings) using an extended version of the CFaiRLLM benchmark that includes intersectional fairness metrics. Baselines will include standard LLM-based recommenders and single-attribute fairness methods. We will measure recommendation quality (NDCG, MAP) alongside intersectional fairness metrics such as intersectional demographic parity and equal opportunity across all attribute combinations.

Dynamic Fairness Adaptation with User Fe.Problem: Static fairness interventions in LLM-based recommender systems fail to adapt to changing user preferences and societal norms, potentially leading to outdated or misaligned fairness criteria over time.
Dynamic Fairness Adaptation with User Fe.Existing Methods: Most fairness approaches for recommender systems use fixed fairness constraints or objectives defined at training time. Existing dynamic methods focus on item-side fairness or single-attribute user fairness.
Dynamic Fairness Adaptation with User Fe.Motivation: User preferences and societal understanding of fairness evolve over time. A dynamic approach that incorporates ongoing user feedback can help recommender systems adapt their fairness criteria to better align with current user expectations and values.
Dynamic Fairness Adaptation with User Fe.Proposed Method: We propose Dynamic Fairness Adaptation (DFA), a novel framework for continuously updating fairness criteria in LLM-based recommenders. DFA consists of three main components: 1) Fairness Perception Elicitation: We design prompts for the LLM to engage users in dialogues about their fairness perceptions, extracting structured representations of user-specific fairness criteria. 2) Adaptive Fairness Aggregation: We develop a mechanism to aggregate individual user fairness perceptions into a global fairness objective, using techniques from social choice theory and multi-stakeholder optimization. This aggregated fairness objective evolves over time as new user feedback is incorporated. 3) Online Fairness Fine-tuning: We introduce a novel online learning algorithm that allows the LLM to continuously fine-tune its representations and outputs to align with the evolving fairness objective. This algorithm balances exploration of new fairness criteria with exploitation of known good practices.
Dynamic Fairness Adaptation with User Fe.Experiment Plan: We will simulate a dynamic recommendation environment using time-stamped datasets (e.g., MovieLens-25M with temporal information). We will compare DFA against static fairness baselines and simpler dynamic approaches. Evaluation metrics will include both recommendation quality (NDCG, MAP) and fairness measures (demographic parity, equal opportunity) computed over sliding time windows. We will also conduct user studies to assess perceived fairness and satisfaction with the evolving recommendations.
